headline_marked: [[Toll road text scam]] steals payment info: FBI warns of widespread smishing texts
headline: Toll road text scam steals payment info: FBI warns of widespread smishing texts
summary: Millions are receiving fake 'unpaid toll' texts demanding small payments via a link. These sophisticated smishing scams harvest credit card, driver's license, and even Social Security numbers.
details: The 'unpaid toll' text scam is widely seen, arriving as a text claiming a small outstanding toll, often around $12.51, with a warning of a $50 late fee. The text looks official, and the link leads to a page designed to mimic a state's toll agency, but it's all fake.

This is a large-scale operation. The FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) received over 2,000 complaints in a month in April 2024, warning the scam was moving state-to-state. The FTC's 2024 data shows text-based fraud cost consumers $470 million, and security researchers found nearly 90,000 dedicated phishing addresses for toll services.

Scammers blast these texts to enormous lists of phone numbers, not targeting specific individuals. The texts use almost identical language and outstanding toll amounts, changing sender numbers by state. Many texts ask you to reply 'Y' before opening the link; this bypasses phone spam protections and confirms your number is active.

The link leads to a convincing replica of a state toll agency site, asking for card details, driver's license, and other identity documents. Everything entered goes directly to criminals. Phished card data is then rapidly loaded into Apple Pay and Google Wallet, allowing criminals to make fraudulent purchases.

The defense is simple: real toll agencies do not collect payments through links in random text messages. Legitimate agencies send bills by mail or use their official apps. Receiving a text about tolls you don't remember, from an unfamiliar state, or with a 'reply Y' demand are clear signs of a scam.

headline: 72% of Anthropic's design questions are AI or ML, vs 38% at OpenAI
summary: Anthropic's most reported design question involves a batched LLM inference API over GPUs, reflecting its deep focus. In contrast, OpenAI's top questions often cover classic system design challenges like building an online chess game.
details: Of Anthropic's 29 reported design questions, 21 (72%) focus on AI systems or Machine Learning. The most frequently reported question involves designing a batched LLM inference API over GPUs, last asked on October 15, 2026.

Anthropic's system design round is typically 55 minutes, without AI assistance, and often requires typing the design into a shared document. This crucial round, usually on the first onsite day, grades APIs, data models, request flow, load handling, and failure cases.

A breakdown of Anthropic's questions shows 12 on AI system design, 9 on ML design, and only 8 on classic system design. Five questions specifically carry a GPU tag, including designing an LLM inference serving platform and a GPU scheduling platform.

OpenAI has 50 reported design questions, compared to Anthropic's 29. While 72% of Anthropic's questions are AI or ML, only 38% of OpenAI's fall into these categories. OpenAI's most reported questions include designing an online chess game, a payment system, and a video generation service on a scarce GPU pool.

Seven design questions are reported at both labs, such as designing an AI prompt playground, an LLM inference serving platform, and a GPU scheduling platform. Candidates interviewing at both companies can leverage this overlap in preparation.

This analysis is based on 29 reported questions for Anthropic and 50 for OpenAI, with data compiled by Land the Lab. The sample size is noted as small, and reports tend to favor software engineering roles, with variations existing across teams and levels.
